title: Roman aqueducts and Persian qanats: how two ancient water systems worked

sources.publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
sources.title: Qanat Irrigated Systems (Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems)
See the Ancient Water Tunnels Below Iran's Desert

facts.text: Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity alone, along a gentle downward slope from the source to the city.
Roman engineers followed the natural slope of the land, even when this meant long detours.
Most of the length of Rome's aqueducts ran underground; arches were only a small share, built where channels crossed valleys.
The Pont du Gard in southern France carried water to the city of Nimes.
Aqueduct water went to public fountains and public baths.
Households that could afford running water paid for a private pipe connection.
Specialized workers cleaned and repaired the aqueduct channels.
The Aqua Virgo is the only ancient aqueduct of Rome that still works; it supplies the Trevi Fountain.
A qanat is an underground tunnel that takes water from an aquifer near hills or mountains and moves it by gravity alone.
The qanat tunnel follows a gentle slope and is linked to the surface by a chain of vertical shafts.
The shafts let air in and let workers remove dust and soil while they dug the tunnels by hand.
Qanat tunnels can be many kilometers long and come out at villages and farms in dry areas.
Because qanats carry water underground, very little is lost to evaporation.
Qanats were developed in ancient Persia (Iran) about 3,000 years ago, and many are still used in Iran.
Qanats need cleaning and repair every year, traditionally organized by local communities.
The qanat idea spread along trade routes as far as Morocco and Spain.

notes: 混合題 mixed-advanced-01 用（2026-10-09 線上查證，只取事實、不取原句）。National Geographic 另提到西班牙 Segovia 水道橋長期使用，所以選文只說「當年供應羅馬城的水道中只剩一條仍在送水」，不說「所有羅馬水道中只剩一條」。坎兒井的年代 FAO 寫 early 800 BC、National Geographic 寫 3,000 年，選文寫 about three thousand years。
